front.title: User-Controlled Device Authorization for MLS using did:webvh Credentials

abstract.t: In Messaging Layer Security (MLS), whoever operates the Authentication Service (AS) decides which devices belong to a user. When providers federate MLS groups, as the More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) work does, every member of a group must accept devices vouched for by every other member's provider. Any one provider can therefore add a device under one of its users' names to any group that user is in. Other members cannot prevent this; at best they detect it after the device has joined.

This document defines an MLS credential type in which the user, not the provider, authorizes each device. The credential carries the user's did:webvh log: a hash-chained, signed history of the user's device keys that any member can verify offline. It also defines group rules that make every member reach the same validity decision and that propagate device revocation through ordinary Commits.

section.name: Why This Document Exists
section.t: MLS delegates identity to an Authentication Service. says a credential is valid when "the AS verifies that the credential's presented identifiers are correctly associated with the signature_key field in the member's LeafNode". The two credential types RFC 9420 defines both put that decision in the hands of a single authority: a "basic" credential is a bare assertion, and an "x509" credential is valid if a trusted certificate authority signed it.

Within one provider, this is the provider's own risk; federation extends it to every member of a shared group. In MIMI , users of several providers share one MLS group, and each provider acts as the AS for its own users. A member on provider B accepts Alice's devices because provider A says they are Alice's. If provider A is compromised or compelled, it can issue a credential binding an attacker's signature key to Alice's identity. The attacker's client joins as one of Alice's devices, receives every epoch secret, and reads all content. calls this a "ghost user". The same technique has been proposed as an exceptional-access mechanism ; federation removes the need for the cooperation of the service the target chose.

The attack is already known. describes it: a compromised AS "could validate a signature key pair (or generate a new one) for an attacker", who could then "join a group as if it were another of the user's clients", and "these attacks could be very difficult to detect". observes that users must "blindly trust their instant messaging service not to add and remove participants" and that "this problem is exacerbated when these systems federate or try to interoperate." This document proposes a way to prevent it.
MLS's forward secrecy and post-compromise security do not help: the ghost is a member by the protocol's own rules.

Interoperability obligations are likely to increase the number of groups that span providers. Article 7 of the Digital Markets Act , for example, requires designated gatekeepers to interoperate with other providers on request.
The mitigations recommends detect the attack rather than prevent it:

list.t: Key transparency "would allow for detection of surreptitiously created false credentials". It needs every client to audit every contact's keys, and MIMI does not require it.
Out-of-band comparison of the per-epoch authentication_secret depends on users comparing values for every member, which few do in large groups.
Showing every membership change to users depends on users noticing an extra device among many.

section.t: In each case the ghost device has already received epoch secrets by the time anyone could notice. Proposals for credentials also keep a single authority:

list.t: X.509 credentials move the authority to a certificate authority, which is chosen or operated by the provider or the user's organization, not by the user.
SD-JWT and SD-CWT credentials add selective disclosure but still rely on one issuer's signature.
An earlier draft used Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) , but only the did:jwk method, which has no history and no way to authorize devices.
surveys certificate hierarchies, webs of trust, cross-signing and Verifiable Credentials for MIMI, but does not define a mechanism.
The key transparency protocol makes bindings auditable, but, as above, detects a ghost device after it has joined.

section.name: What This Document Fixes
section.t: This document takes the decision about which devices belong to a user away from the provider and gives it to keys the user controls. A provider that holds no update key cannot authorize a device.

texttable.title: Trust model before and after
texttable.c: Who can add a device to Alice's identity?
Alice's provider's AS, or anyone who compromises or compels it
Only a holder of one of Alice's did:webvh update keys
How does another member verify Alice's device?
Verifies Alice's signed, hash-chained log, offline
Can a provider add a device without Alice's keys?
Yes. Other members can detect it only after the device has joined
It cannot authorize a new key. It can still replay a revoked device's old KeyPackages to a group that has not seen the revocation ()
How is a revoked device removed from a group?
The Commit that carries Alice's newer log MUST remove it
Can two members disagree about a credential's validity?
Yes, if their AS policies differ
No: credential validity depends only on the credential and the group's state ()

section.t: The provider keeps its roles as transport, KeyPackage directory and, optionally, host of the user's did:webvh log. None of those roles lets it change which devices are Alice's.

section.name: What This Document Does Not Fix

list.t: First contact. This document does not say how Bob learns which DID is Alice's. Once Bob has pinned it, substitution is detectable (). Discovery is out of scope.
Custody. If the provider holds Alice's update keys, it can authorize devices and this credential adds nothing ().
Metadata. The Delivery Service (DS) and the MIMI hub still see group membership and timing. This credential reveals more device history to them, not less ().
Ordering, censorship and hub trust. A hub can still delay or drop Commits, including Commits that remove a revoked device.

section.name: Conventions and Definitions
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.
This document uses the terms from and . In addition:

dd.t: The user who holds the update keys of a did:webvh DID and whose devices its DID document lists.
The did:webvh DID Log, the did.jsonl file defined in .
The integer before the dash in a log entry's versionId.
The last entry of a log carried in a credential.
Log A is a prefix of log B if B has at least as many entries as A and the versionId values of B's first entries equal those of A's entries, in order. Byte equality of the logs is not required.
Of several logs, the one whose head has the highest version number.
The self-certifying identifier of a did:webvh DID: the value of the scid parameter of the log's first entry. It does not change when the DID moves to a different host.
For an SCID S, the entry for S in the group's did_webvh_heads GroupContext extension (): the highest log version the group has accepted for S, and the keys that version authorizes.

An Ed25519 public key given by a verification method in a DID document that meets all of the following: its type is Multikey and its controller is the document's id; its publicKeyMultibase begins with z and base58btc-decodes to exactly 34 bytes, the prefix 0xed 0x01 followed by a 32-byte public key in the format of ; and it is in the document's authentication verification relationship, either embedded there or referenced by identifier (, ). A relative reference is resolved against the document's id as specifies. A reference that does not resolve to a verification method in the same document, and a verification method that fails any of these conditions, authorizes no key; neither makes the document invalid.

section.name: Overview
section.t: The user's DID document is the list of the user's devices. Each device has its own MLS signature key, and each such key is listed in the DID document as an authorized key. Adding a device means appending a log entry that lists its key. That entry must be signed by an update key. So the provider cannot add a device unless it holds an update key.

This document uses did:webvh only as a specified format for a self-certifying, signed, hash-chained key log. It uses no DID resolution, DID URL dereferencing, Verifiable Credentials or resolver infrastructure.

Each device's LeafNode carries a credential containing the user's whole log, up to a head that authorizes that device's key. Members verify the log with no network access. Members do not consult the published log location, a resolver, witnesses or watchers during validation.

Revocation works through the group itself. When Alice revokes a device, one of her remaining devices appends an entry that drops the revoked key, then sends a Commit whose UpdatePath carries the new log. The group records the newest head it has accepted for each SCID in a GroupContext extension, and that record never moves backwards. The rules in require the Commit that raises the record to remove every leaf whose key the new head no longer authorizes. Every member checks the same rules against the same tree and GroupContext, so they all accept or reject the Commit alike.

section.name: The did:webvh Credential
section.t: This document adds a new credential type, did_webvh, to the Credential structure from :

dd.t: The DID Log in the did.jsonl format of , from the first entry through the head, with no entries omitted and none after the head. It MUST NOT be longer than 1,048,576 bytes.
The did-witness.json content defined in , holding the witness proofs for the carried entries. It MUST be empty if no carried entry has active witnesses, and MUST NOT be longer than 1,048,576 bytes.

section.t: The size limits are fixed so that every member applies the same limit. A limit that differed between implementations would let one member accept a credential that another rejects.

This document supports only cipher suites whose signature scheme is Ed25519, such as MLS_128_DHKEMX25519_AES128GCM_SHA256_Ed25519 (0x0001) and MLS_128_DHKEMX25519_CHACHA20POLY1305_SHA256_Ed25519 (0x0003). A did_webvh credential in a group using any other cipher suite MUST be rejected.

section.name: Validation
section.t: A did_webvh credential MUST be validated at each event listed in . Validation has three parts: verifying the log (), binding the log to the LeafNode (), and checking it against the rest of the group (). A credential that fails any check MUST be rejected, together with the message or object that introduced it.

section.name: Log Verification
section.t: The verifier MUST verify did_log and witness_file with the Read (Resolve) verification steps of , with these changes:

list.t: The verifier treats did_log as the complete published log and witness_file as the complete witness file. It MUST NOT fetch either from the network, and MUST NOT consult watchers or resolver caches. The DID being resolved is the id of the head's DID document.
The method parameter of the first entry MUST be did:webvh:1.0, and no later entry may set method to any other value. A log that does MUST be rejected, so that every member applies one set of rules.
The verifier MUST NOT compare versionTime with its own clock. All other versionTime checks still apply, including that values strictly increase. The ttl parameter has no effect on validation.
Witness proofs MUST be verified as specifies for every entry that has active witnesses. Proofs in witness_file for versionIds not in did_log are ignored.
After every entry has been processed, the active value of the deactivated parameter MUST be false, and no entry may follow an entry that sets it to true.
Every carried entry MUST verify. The option gives resolvers to treat a log as valid up to its first invalid entry is not used.
The verifier MUST apply the profile in .

section.t: Change 3 is needed because rejects entries more than a tolerance into the future relative to "the resolver's current time". Clocks differ between members, so applying that check would let members disagree about validity. Strict ordering of versionTime values does not depend on the clock and is kept.

section.name: did:webvh Profile
section.t: leaves some choices to implementations. Members that chose differently could disagree about a credential's validity, so this document fixes them:

dd.t: did_log MUST be UTF-8 JSON Lines: one JSON object per line, each line ending in a single LF (0x0A), with no blank lines and nothing after the last LF. Each log entry, and witness_file, MUST be I-JSON ; in particular, an object with duplicate member names is rejected. versionTime values MUST have the form YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ. The version number MUST NOT have leading zeros.
A parameter whose value is null MUST be rejected, although lets resolvers accept it.
The proof member of each entry MUST be an array containing exactly one proof. The created and expires properties of log and witness proofs are not compared with any clock.
A witness proof that fails verification is ignored. An entry's witness requirement is met only if valid proofs from at least the threshold number of distinct witnesses cover it.
The portability rules of , including that portable can only be set in the first entry and that a moved DID lists its previous DID in alsoKnownAs, MUST be checked for every entry.
The DID string MUST match the method-specific identifier syntax of using only ASCII letters, digits, hyphens and dots. No internationalized domain name processing is performed.

section.name: Binding to the LeafNode
section.t: The signature_key of the LeafNode containing the credential MUST equal the 32-byte public key of an authorized key in the head's DID document.
The SCID of the log is the credential's identity. The DID string can change if the controller moves the DID, but the SCID cannot.
A did_webvh credential MUST NOT appear in the external_senders GroupContext extension. A GroupContextExtensions proposal that would put one there MUST be rejected.

section.name: The Heads Extension
section.t: A client that lists did_webvh in the credentials field of its LeafNode capabilities MUST list did_webvh_heads in the extensions field and MUST implement the rules in . A GroupContext that contains did_webvh_heads MUST also contain a required_capabilities extension that lists did_webvh_heads in extension_types and did_webvh in credential_types (), so that every member enforces the rules. A group whose tree contains a did_webvh credential MUST carry the did_webvh_heads GroupContext extension, and a group that carries it MUST NOT remove it:

dd.t: The SCID, as the ASCII value of the first entry's scid parameter.
The versionId of the recorded head.

The 32-byte public keys of every authorized key in the recorded head's DID document, each as a SignaturePublicKey, sorted in ascending lexicographic order of the key bytes (not of their encoding), with no duplicates.

section.t: heads MUST contain an entry for each SCID that appears in a leaf of the ratchet tree. It also keeps the entry for every SCID the group has recorded before, even when no leaf with that SCID remains: an entry is never removed. At most one entry has a given scid. Entries are sorted in ascending lexicographic byte order of scid, a shorter value that is a prefix of a longer one sorting first.

The extension lets the group remember a revocation after every leaf that carried the revoking log has left, and after every device of that user has left. Without it, the newest log the group knew about could leave with the last device that carried it, and an older log would make a revoked key valid again. Because the extension is part of the GroupContext, a new member receives it in the Welcome, and it feeds the key schedule.

section.name: When the Rules Apply
section.t: When a member receives a KeyPackage, an Add proposal or an Update proposal, it verifies the log () and the binding to the LeafNode () only. The group rules depend on every proposal in a Commit, so they are checked once per Commit, against the ratchet tree and GroupContext that result from applying all of the Commit's proposals and its UpdatePath. A member joining through a Welcome or an external Commit checks them against the tree and GroupContext it receives.

section.name: Expected Heads
section.t: For each SCID S that appears in a leaf of the resulting tree, let R be the reference entry for S: the entry for S in the previous epoch's did_webvh_heads, if any. Let L be the newest log among the resulting tree's credentials with SCID S. The expected entry for S is computed as follows:

list.t: If R exists and L's head version number is not greater than R's, the expected entry is R.

If R exists and L's head version number is greater than R's, L MUST contain an entry whose versionId is R's version_id; a Commit for which it does not MUST be rejected. The expected entry has L's head versionId and the authorized keys of L's head DID document.
If R does not exist, the expected entry has L's head versionId and the authorized keys of L's head DID document.

section.t: For each SCID S that has an entry in the previous epoch's did_webvh_heads but appears in no leaf of the resulting tree, the expected entry is that previous entry, unchanged.

The did_webvh_heads extension in the resulting GroupContext MUST contain exactly the expected entries. A Commit that changes the expected value MUST therefore include a GroupContextExtensions proposal that sets it. A Commit that only removes leaves never changes the expected value.

section.name: Rules
section.t: The following MUST hold for the resulting tree and GroupContext. A Commit, Welcome or GroupInfo for which any of them fails MUST be rejected.

dd.t: did_webvh_heads contains exactly the expected entries.
Every credential with SCID S whose head version number is at least R's contains an entry whose versionId is R's version_id. Every credential with SCID S whose head is newer than R's is a prefix of L.
Every leaf with SCID S has a signature_key in the authorized_keys of the recorded head of S.

section.t: A Commit that raises the recorded head of S to a version that no longer authorizes some of S's leaves therefore has to remove those leaves in the same Commit. Some consequences follow from without further rules:

list.t: A committer whose own key the new head does not authorize cannot send that Commit, because a Commit cannot remove its committer (). Another member has to commit it, for example by committing an Update proposal, sent by one of the user's other devices, that carries the new log.

An external Commit cannot carry a GroupContextExtensions proposal, so it is valid only if it leaves did_webvh_heads unchanged. A device can rejoin by external Commit only if its key is already authorized by the recorded head and its log is not newer than the recorded head. A client whose SCID has no entry in did_webvh_heads, which includes every new user, cannot join by external Commit and has to be added by an existing member ().

section.t: A member joining by Welcome has no previous epoch, so it cannot compute the expected entries. It instead checks that did_webvh_heads has an entry for each SCID in the tree, in sorted order with no duplicates, and the consistency and authorization rules, taking R for each SCID from the GroupContext it receives. It also checks that no leaf's head version number is greater than the recorded version for its SCID. For each recorded head that some leaf's log contains as its head, it also checks that authorized_keys matches that DID document. For an entry that no leaf carries, including the entry of an SCID with no leaves, the joiner relies on the GroupContext, which the existing members agreed on through the key schedule.

section.name: Successor Credentials
section.t: For the replacement check in , a did_webvh credential is a valid successor to an earlier did_webvh credential if it has the same SCID and the earlier credential's log is a prefix of the new one.

A leaf whose credential carries an older head than the recorded head stays valid as long as its key is in the recorded authorized_keys. Devices do not need to update their credentials each time another device of the same user is added.

section.name: Reference Identifiers
section.t: has the application compare presented identifiers with reference identifiers. For this credential, the presented identifier is the SCID. Applications SHOULD pin the SCID for each contact the first time it is learned, SHOULD compare it on every later credential for that contact, and MUST alert the user if the SCID for a contact changes. Applications SHOULD display the DID string from the head, because the SCID alone means nothing to a person.

list.t: The new device generates an MLS signature key pair.

A holder of a key authorized to sign the next entry appends a log entry whose DID document lists the new key as an authorized key. If witnesses are active, the holder collects the threshold of witness proofs.
The holder SHOULD publish the updated log and witness file at the location defines, so that new contacts can learn the DID. Group members do not need the published copy.
The new device publishes KeyPackages whose credential carries the updated log.

section.name: Revoking a Device

list.t: A holder of a key authorized to sign the next entry appends an entry whose DID document no longer lists the revoked key.

For every group the user belongs to, one of the user's remaining devices sends a Commit whose UpdatePath LeafNode carries the new log, together with Remove proposals for the revoked device's leaves and a GroupContextExtensions proposal that updates did_webvh_heads. The rules in make the Remove mandatory.

section.t: The revocation reaches a group when one of the controller's own devices commits to it, not when a resolver notices. covers the case where none of the controller's devices is in the group.

section.name: Custody of Update Keys
section.t: This credential moves authority to whoever holds the updateKeys. Update keys SHOULD be held only on the user's devices and in offline recovery storage, and the provider SHOULD NOT hold them. A deployment in which the provider holds update keys gives the provider the same power the AS has today. A member cannot detect such a deployment from the credential.

Controllers SHOULD enable pre-rotation by setting nextKeyHashes, and SHOULD include among the committed hashes, in every entry, the hash of a recovery key kept offline. Controllers SHOULD NOT commit the hash of a key that has already been revealed. Under pre-rotation, each entry must be signed by a key whose hash the previous entry committed to, so an attacker needs one of those committed next keys, not just a key that has already been used. Controllers SHOULD NOT make every device an update key: any device that holds one can add or revoke all the others. Keys listed in authentication SHOULD be used only as MLS device keys, and update keys SHOULD NOT appear in authentication, because every authorized key there is accepted as a device.

Two update-key holders that append entries at the same time fork the log, which names as a known risk. A group that has recorded one branch rejects the other. The device whose entry lost can recover by appending a new entry to the winning branch. If different groups have recorded different branches, though, no later log can satisfy both groups, and the user has to be removed from one of them and added back once its record is gone. Controllers SHOULD therefore send every update through a single writer, or use witnesses with a threshold greater than half the number of witnesses. forbids a witness from signing two children of the same parent entry, but two disjoint sets of witnesses that each meet a lower threshold can approve different children.

section.name: Negotiation and Mandating the Credential
section.t: A client that supports this credential type lists did_webvh in the credentials field of its LeafNode capabilities. A group, or a MIMI room through its policy, can require this credential type for every member by listing it in the required_capabilities GroupContext extension and rejecting other credential types.

In a group that also admits basic or x509 credentials, those leaves keep the trust model of their AS, and the gap in remains for them. Applications SHOULD indicate to users which members are authenticated by a did_webvh credential.

section.name: Open Issues
section.t: RFC Editor: please remove this section before publication.
The author would like the working group's view on these questions:

list.t: Extension or component. Carrying the record as a component of the app_data_dictionary extension , updated by AppDataUpdate proposals, would let an external Commit or an external sender update it. That would allow new users to join by external Commit, which this document does not, and would avoid a GroupContextExtensions proposal in every Commit that changes the record.
ReInit and branching. Neither carries the record into the new group, so a revocation known to the old group can be lost. A ReInit could be required to carry did_webvh_heads in its extensions.

Revocation without a controller's device. A newer log reaches a group only through a leaf that carries it. A proposal that carries a newer log as evidence would let any member raise the record, and would give a way to propagate deactivation.
Other signature schemes. Supporting cipher suites whose signature scheme is not Ed25519, such as 0x0002 with P-256, would admit deployments that need them.

Cost of GroupContextExtensions. Because a GroupContextExtensions proposal replaces the whole extension list and only one is allowed per Commit, a pending GroupContextExtensions proposal from another party cannot be combined with a change to the record.

Record growth. Entries are never removed, so the record grows with every user who has ever been a member. A way to retire entries without losing revocations, for example after the user's log has been deactivated, may be needed for long-lived groups.

Encoding without DIDs. The mechanism does not depend on DIDs. What it needs is a key the user holds that authorizes each device, and a signed, hash-chained history of those authorizations, so that every member can verify additions and revocations offline. did:webvh is one existing encoding of that history. The same property could be built from IETF work instead: a CWT or SD-CWT credential issued by the user's key , with the history as a sequence of signed statements in the style of ; a log format defined directly in TLS presentation language; or the user's devices acting as one virtual client , so that only an existing device can add another. In each case, key transparency would complement this design, not replace it. It detects a device the provider adds, where this design prevents one, and it can cover first contact. The author would like the working group's view on which encoding to use.

section.name: Provider-Issued Devices
section.t: A provider without an update key cannot produce a log entry that authorizes a new key, because every entry needs an eddsa-jcs-2022 signature by an authorized update key . It also cannot present an altered history, because entries are hash-chained and the SCID is derived from the first entry. Whoever hosts the published log has no more power than the provider: members never read the published log during validation.

section.name: Pervasive Monitoring
section.t: states that "pervasive monitoring is a technical attack that should be mitigated in the design of IETF protocols, where possible", and calls for protocols that make it "significantly more expensive or infeasible". Adding a ghost device targets one user, but the capability exists in every room. A single compromised or compelled provider can use it in every room that contains one of its users, without any change visible in the MLS protocol. Federation adds every other provider's users to the set of people exposed to that one provider.

In groups that require the did_webvh credential, this document removes that capability for existing identities: a provider cannot authorize a new device under a user's SCID while the group holds that SCID's record. A provider that wants to add a device to a user's identity needs one of the user's update keys, and any entry it creates stays in a log that every member of the group holds. This document does not stop a party that can add members from adding a different identity, or from substituting a DID at first contact ().

section.name: Update Key Compromise
section.t: An attacker who can sign a valid next entry can add a device, or revoke the user's honest devices and so get them removed from groups by the rules in . With pre-rotation active, that requires one of the keys committed in nextKeyHashes, not merely a key already used. Either action leaves an entry in a log that every member of each affected group holds. The user's own devices SHOULD alert the user when a log entry appears that none of the user's devices created.

If the attacker branches from an entry older than a group's recorded head, the group rejects the branch. If the attacker extends the current head, the group accepts the extension, because it is indistinguishable from an honest update. Detection then rests on the user's devices.

section.name: Withheld or Stale Logs
section.t: lists "truncation or withholding of log entries" as an attack on resolvers: a host presents an older valid prefix of the log to hide a revocation. This credential has no resolver, so the host has nothing to withhold from. The newest log reaches a group when any of the controller's devices sends a Commit.

Once a group has accepted a revoking log, the recorded head keeps the revoked key out even after the device that committed it leaves, and after every device of that user has left, because entries are never removed.

The remaining exposure is a group that never saw the revocation. That includes a group that contains a revoked device of the controller but none of the controller's other devices, and any group to which the provider, acting as KeyPackage directory, delivers one of the revoked device's old KeyPackages. Nobody in such a group has the newer log, so the revoked device stays until someone removes it. Clients SHOULD remember the highest log version they have verified for each SCID, across all groups, and SHOULD refuse to add a KeyPackage whose log is older, which mirrors the cache-and-compare mitigation in . This check is local, so it guides what a client proposes, not what the group accepts. Applications SHOULD also let a controller's device that is not in a group send the newer log to that group's members, for example through the MIMI hub. Detecting revocations without any device of the controller present needs an external freshness mechanism such as key transparency , which is out of scope.

section.name: First Contact
section.t: The SCID protects a contact once it has been pinned. It does not protect the first lookup, when an attacker who controls discovery can give Bob a DID it created itself. Applications SHOULD offer out-of-band comparison of the SCID, for example by QR code, as they do today for safety numbers.

section.name: Delivery Service and Hub
section.t: A DS or MIMI hub cannot forge or alter a did_webvh credential. It can delay or drop the Commit that carries a revocation, which extends the window during which a revoked device remains a member. This credential does not change the hub's ability to censor.

section.name: Deterministic Validation
section.t: MLS assumes that all members agree on which credentials are valid. If they disagree, they disagree about the membership of the group. This document removes the inputs under its control that could differ between members: network fetches, the verifier's clock, implementation-specific size limits, the choices leaves open (), and did:webvh versions other than 1.0. Credential validity is then a function of the credential bytes, the ratchet tree and the previous epoch's GroupContext. Two inputs remain outside this document: the reference-identifier check of , which is application policy (), and the RECOMMENDED LeafNode lifetime check of , which uses the clock.

section.name: Resource Use
section.t: A log grows by one entry for each device change. Each leaf carries the whole log, so a user with many devices in a large group adds repeated copies to the tree. Each leaf can carry up to 2 MiB (log and witness file), so the ratchet tree in a Welcome or GroupInfo of a large group can be very large, and a joiner validates every leaf's log, each entry with its own signature verification. Implementations SHOULD verify a log shared by several leaves once. The did_webvh_heads record grows by one entry for each user who has ever been a member and is never pruned. The 1,048,576-byte limits bound the cost of a malicious log. This document defines no way to compact a log.

section.name: Privacy Considerations
section.t: Every member of a group, and any DS or hub that can see LeafNodes, learns the controller's whole device history: how many devices the controller has had, when each was added and removed, the domain hosting the DID, and any witnesses. So does anyone who can fetch the user's KeyPackages from a directory. A basic or X.509 credential reveals much less.
The SCID is a stable identifier across groups and providers, so it lets those parties correlate a user's memberships. Users who need separate identities in different contexts need separate DIDs.
Validation makes no network requests, so it does not tell the log host or any resolver who is checking whom.

section.t: RFC Editor: please replace "RFC XXXX" with the RFC number of this document.

abstract.t: Messaging applications are increasingly making use of end-to-end security mechanisms to ensure that messages are only accessible to the communicating endpoints, and not to any servers involved in delivering messages. Establishing keys to provide such protections is challenging for group chat settings, in which more than two clients need to agree on a key but may not be online at the same time. In this document, we specify a key establishment protocol that provides efficient asynchronous group key establishment with forward secrecy (FS) and post-compromise security (PCS) for groups in size ranging from two to thousands.

This document describes elliptic curve signature scheme Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA). The algorithm is instantiated with recommended parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves. An example implementation and test vectors are provided.
I-JSON (short for "Internet JSON") is a restricted profile of JSON designed to maximize interoperability and increase confidence that software can process it successfully with predictable results.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.
Pervasive monitoring is a technical attack that should be mitigated in the design of IETF protocols, where possible.

The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol (RFC 9420) provides a group key agreement protocol for messaging applications. MLS is designed to protect against eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery, and to provide forward secrecy (FS) and post-compromise security (PCS).

This document describes the architecture for using MLS in a general secure group messaging infrastructure and defines the security goals for MLS. It provides guidance on building a group messaging system and discusses security and privacy trade-offs offered by multiple security mechanisms that are part of the MLS protocol (e.g., frequency of public encryption key rotation). The document also provides guidance for parts of the infrastructure that are not standardized by MLS and are instead left to the application.

While the recommendations of this document are not mandatory to follow in order to interoperate at the protocol level, they affect the overall security guarantees that are achieved by a messaging application. This is especially true in the case of active adversaries that are able to compromise clients, the Delivery Service (DS), or the Authentication Service (AS).

front.title: More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) Identity Concepts

abstract.t: This document explores the problem space in instant messaging (IM) identity interoperability when using end-to-end encryption, for example with the MLS (Message Layer Security) Protocol. It also describes naming schemes for different types of IM identifiers.

front.title: More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) using HTTPS and MLS

abstract.t: This document specifies the More Instant Messaging Interoperability (MIMI) transport protocol, which allows users of different messaging providers to interoperate in group chats (rooms), including to send and receive messages, share room policy, and add participants to and remove participants from rooms. MIMI describes messages between providers, leaving most aspects of the provider-internal client- server communication up to the provider. MIMI integrates the Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol to provide end-to-end security assurances, including authentication of protocol participants, confidentiality of messages exchanged within a room, and agreement on the state of the room.

While there are several established protocols for end-to-end encryption, relatively little attention has been given to securely distributing the end-user public keys for such encryption. As a result, these protocols are often still vulnerable to eavesdropping by active attackers. Key Transparency is a protocol for distributing sensitive cryptographic information, such as public keys, in a way that reliably either prevents interference or detects that it occurred in a timely manner.

front.title: Messaging Layer Security Credentials using Selective Disclosure JSON and CBOR Web Tokens

abstract.t: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol contains Credentials used to authenticate an MLS client with a signature key pair. Selective Disclosure CBOR Web Tokens (SD-CWT) and Selective Disclosure JSON Web Tokens (SD-JWT) define token formats where the holder can selectively reveal claims about itself with strong integrity protection and cryptographic binding to the holder's key. This document defines MLS credentials for both these token types.

This specification defines two new kinds of credentials for use within the Message Layer Security (MLS) credential framework: UserInfo Verifiable Credentials and multi-credentials. UserInfo Verifiable Credentials allow clients to present credentials that associate OpenID Connect attributes to a signature key pair held by the client. Multi-credentials allow clients to present authenticated attributes from multiple sources, or to present credentials in different formats to support groups with heterogeneous credential support.

The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) protocol is an asynchronous group authenticated key exchange protocol. MLS provides a number of capabilities to applications, as well as several extension points internal to the protocol. This document provides a consolidated application API, guidance for how the protocol's extension points should be used, and a few concrete examples of both core protocol extensions and uses of the application API.

front.title: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains

abstract.t: Traceability in supply chains is a growing security concern. While Verifiable Data Structures (VDSs) have addressed specific issues, such as equivocation over digital certificates, they lack a universal architecture for all supply chains. This document defines such an architecture for single-issuer signed statement transparency. It ensures extensibility and interoperability between different transparency services as well as compliance with various auditing procedures and regulatory requirements.

This document describes a method that allows multiple MLS clients to emulate a virtual MLS client. A virtual client allows multiple emulator clients to jointly participate in an MLS group under a single leaf. Depending on the design of the application, virtual clients can help hide metadata and improve performance.

dl.dt: Why not an SD-JWT or SD-CWT credential:

dd.t: A token needs an issuer, and an issuer is the single authority this document removes. The did:webvh log certifies itself.

dl.dt: Why not resolve the DID during validation:

dd.t: Resolution brings back the stale-log attack, tells the log host who is checking whom, and lets members who resolve at different times disagree.

dl.dt: Why the DID document lists device keys directly:

dd.t: A separate signed statement binding a device to the DID would be a second format to validate. Using the authentication relationship means a device is authorized exactly when the user's log says so.

Every additional method or version is another set of rules that all members must apply identically. Ed25519 matches the mandatory-to-implement MLS cipher suite and needs no conversion between key formats. Other methods and other signature schemes can be specified in future documents ().
